# Interpolation Schemes for Volume Rendering

Also called: Fourier window, Interpolation Schemes for Frequency Domain Volume Rendering, Reconstruction Filters, Sample-and-hold, Zero-order interpolation, Zeroth-order interpolation, box filter

## Overview
Interpolation schemes for volume rendering reconstruct a continuous scalar field from discrete voxel data to estimate values at arbitrary query positions during ray casting [S1, S2, S3, unofficial]. The choice of scheme defines the trade-off between computational complexity, spatial extent (number of neighbors), and frequency response (aliasing vs. blurring) [S1, S2, unofficial]. Unlike [Nearest Neighbor Sampling](11694-nearest-neighbor-sampling.md), which produces severe staircase artifacts, higher-order methods like [Trilinear Interpolation](1531-trilinear-interpolation.md) and [Fast tri-cubic interpolation](848-fast-tri-cubic-interpolation.md) provide smoother results, while [Frequency Domain Volume Rendering with Sinc Resampling](826-frequency-domain-volume-rendering-with-sinc-resampling.md) achieves theoretical optimality by operating in the Fourier domain.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family map a query position $\mathbf{p}$ in [voxel space](#3074-voxel-space.md) to a scalar value $V(\mathbf{p})$ by combining a finite set of neighboring voxel values $V_i$ using a set of weights $w_i(\mathbf{p})$:
$$
V(\mathbf{p}) = \sum_{i} w_i(\mathbf{p}) V_i
$$
The weights are derived from a reconstruction kernel $h(\mathbf{z})$, where $\mathbf{z}$ is the distance from the query point to the sample center [G]. The choice of kernel defines the trade-off between computational complexity, spatial extent (number of neighbors), and frequency response (aliasing vs. blurring) [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Frequency Domain Volume Rendering with Sinc Resampling](826-frequency-domain-volume-rendering-with-sinc-resampling.md)
[Frequency Domain Volume Rendering](#952-frequency-domain-volume-rendering.md) ([FD method](#826-frequency-domain-volume-rendering-with-sinc-resampling.md)) is a volume rendering algorithm that performs resampling using the ideal interpolation filter (sinc) to achieve the best theoretical quality, exploiting signal processing ideas such as the shifting theorem, the packing theorem, and the derivative theorem. It solves the problem of blurring artifacts associated with spatial domain interpolation, particularly for large zoom factors, by performing resampling (zooming and shearing) in the frequency domain using [Fourier transforms](#2288-fourier-transform.md). Unlike [Trilinear Interpolation](1531-trilinear-interpolation.md) or [Fast tri-cubic interpolation](848-fast-tri-cubic-interpolation.md) which operate in the spatial domain, this method allows perfect reconstruction of the original signal if the sampling was done according to the Nyquist criteria.

### [Fast tri-cubic interpolation](848-fast-tri-cubic-interpolation.md)
[Fast tri-cubic interpolation](#848-fast-tri-cubic-interpolation.md) is a GPU-optimized reconstruction scheme that evaluates a tri-cubic B-spline filter using significantly fewer texture fetches than the theoretical 64 nearest-neighbor lookups required by the full kernel support. It solves the problem of high computational cost in higher-order volume rendering by leveraging GPU linear [texture filtering](#4541-mipmap-filtering.md) and separable kernel [decomposition](#7254-decomposition.md) to reduce the operation to eight tri-linear texture fetches per sample. It sets itself apart from standard [tri-cubic interpolation](#1077-tri-cubic-interpolation.md) by avoiding on-the-fly kernel tile multiplication and from [Trilinear Interpolation](1531-trilinear-interpolation.md) by providing $C^2$ continuous, higher-order accuracy with reduced aliasing, albeit at the cost of increased oversmoothing compared to non-interpolating methods like [Prefiltered Reconstruction](11114-prefiltered-reconstruction.md).

### [Bilinear Interpolation](858-bilinear-interpolation.md)
[Bilinear interpolation](#858-bilinear-interpolation.md) is a reconstruction scheme that estimates a scalar value at an arbitrary 2D coordinate by performing linear interpolation in both spatial dimensions using the four nearest grid points. It serves as the fundamental building block for higher-order methods like trilinear interpolation and is used in volume rendering to sample scalar fields on 2D planes or to approximate 3D values by restricting sampling to cell faces. It sets itself apart from [nearest neighbor interpolation](#5891-nearest-neighbor-interpolation.md) by providing continuous, first-order smoothness, and from trilinear interpolation by operating in two dimensions rather than three, requiring fewer neighbor lookups (4 vs 8).

### [Hardware Interpolation Approximation](1027-hardware-interpolation-approximation.md)
[Hardware Interpolation Approximation](#1027-hardware-interpolation-approximation.md) approximates the [volume rendering integral](#8682-volume-rendering-integral.md) by assuming linear interpolation along ray segments, resulting in piecewise bilinear or trilinear interpolation depending on polygon subdivision. It sets itself apart from its siblings by relying on view-dependent, hardware-enforced piecewise interpolation determined by polygon subdivision, rather than explicit, view-independent kernel-based reconstruction.

### [Trilinear Interpolation](1531-trilinear-interpolation.md)
Trilinear interpolation estimates the scalar value at an arbitrary point within a voxel grid by computing a weighted average of the values of the 8 surrounding voxels, based on their distances to the sample point. It solves the problem of discretization artifacts (blockiness) inherent in [nearest-neighbor sampling](#1151-nearest-neighbor-density-lookup.md) by providing a continuous, first-order approximation of the underlying scalar field. It produces softer, higher-quality images than nearest-neighbor interpolation but requires approximately 5 times more computation time.

### [Inverse Distance Weighted Interpolation](2336-inverse-distance-weighted-interpolation.md)
Inverse Distance Weighted (IDW) Interpolation is a spatial [interpolation method](#10526-interpolation-methods.md) that generates a continuous 3D scalar field from discrete sample points by weighting nearby samples by the inverse of their distance raised to a power. It solves the problem of reconstructing a volume from irregular or sparse data (e.g., drill-hole assays) where grid-aligned interpolation schemes like trilinear are not directly applicable. While often applied to arbitrary point sets, specific implementations restrict the neighborhood to the eight vertices of the grid cell containing the query point. It does not guarantee $C^0$ continuity along interior faces of the grid.

### Variable Gaussian Blurring
Variable Gaussian Blurring is a reconstruction technique used to reduce visible artifacts from the discrete sampled nature of volume models, specifically false low frequencies caused by the Nyquist limit [S6, unofficial]. It involves applying variable Gaussian blurring to the source volume models before or during reconstruction to high-resolution 2D images [S6, unofficial]. The Nyquist Limit is defined as half the sampling rate, and infinite sampling of continuous surfaces is the only way to completely avoid artifacts [S6, unofficial].

### Barycentric Color Interpolation for Voxels
Barycentric Color Interpolation for Voxels interpolates vertex colors to a voxel center by treating the voxel center as a point inside the triangle and weighting the vertex colors by the areas of the sub-triangles formed with the voxel center [S7, unofficial]. The formula is $c = c_1 \cdot (A_2 / A) + c_2 \cdot (A_3 / A) + c_3 \cdot (A_1 / A)$, where $A_1 = \text{area}(v_1, v_2, P)$, $A_2 = \text{area}(v_2, v_3, P)$, $A_3 = \text{area}(v_3, v_1, P)$, $A = A_1 + A_2 + A_3$, and $P$ is the voxel center [S7, unofficial].

### Adaptive Interpolation for Isosurface Detection
[Adaptive Interpolation](#861-adaptive-filter-size-for-rendering-time-reduction.md) for Isosurface Detection interpolates input volume along rays at a predetermined sampling rate. It uses non-binary classifiers to adjust the acceptable density range for an isovalue surface based on data change rate [S3, unofficial]. When data values change slowly, a narrow range of acceptable values is used for the isovalue surface. When data values change rapidly, a wide range is used to avoid missing the surface [S3, unofficial]. It supports user selection of interpolation: nearest-neighbor (preview), linear (day-to-day), cubic (publication-quality) [S3, unofficial].

### Interpolation Schemes for Projection-Slice Resampling
Interpolation Schemes for Projection-Slice Resampling are resampling filters applied to extracted projection-slices to control ghosting artifacts and rendering quality during Fourier volume rendering [S8]. [Point-sampling](#2382-ray-point-sampling.md) (nearest-neighbour) filter clamps missing samples to the nearest available value, causing apparent ghosting artifacts when the volume is rotated [S8]. Trilinear interpolation filter reduces replica intensities and ghosting artifacts compared to point-sampling, with similar performance for slice sizes $\le 512^2$ but higher cost for larger volumes [S8]. Hamming windowed-sinc interpolation filter with width 5 is a high-order reconstruction filter that maximally reduces ghosting artifacts when combined with [zero-padding](#6382-zero-padding-for-aliasing-reduction.md) [S8]. Point-sampling and trilinear interpolation have nearly identical performance for slice sizes $\le 512^2$, but trilinear incurs higher performance overhead for larger volumes [S8].

## Background
The concept of interpolation in volume rendering emerged alongside the development of [direct volume ray casting](#19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md). Early methods relied on nearest-neighbor interpolation due to its simplicity, but this resulted in severe artifacts such as staircase effects and blockiness [S1, S3, S4, unofficial]. As hardware capabilities increased, higher-order methods like trilinear and cubic interpolation became feasible, offering improved visual quality by eliminating these artifacts [S4, S5, unofficial]. The introduction of frequency domain techniques, such as those by Westover (1990) and Levoy (1990), allowed for more sophisticated reconstruction filters, including windowed sinc filters, to address aliasing and blurring issues more effectively [S4, S5, unofficial]. Modern implementations often leverage GPU hardware [acceleration](#18-acceleration.md) to optimize these computations, particularly for higher-order filters like tri-cubic B-splines [S1, S5, unofficial].
